headline: Not yet. Stocks end flat as the IMF tallies $650B of circular AI debt.
summary: The S&P 500 closed Tuesday 13 October at 7,805.45, down 0.02%, as chips fell again on Chinese memory competition and Seoul's Kospi lost 5.46%. The IMF named an AI correction a top global risk and counted $650B of debt in circular AI deals.

analysis: Wall Street closed Tuesday 13 October almost unchanged: the S&P 500 at 7,805.45 (−0.02%), the Nasdaq at 27,204.38 (−0.15%) and the Dow at 51,670.10 (−0.35%), while JPMorgan earned $5.57 a share against a $5.90 estimate. [1] Chips kept sliding: by mid-afternoon Micron was down about 5.8%, AMD 3.3% and Nvidia 1.3%, after China's CXMT announced progress on a new, denser memory-cell design. [1][4] Seoul's Kospi closed down 5.46%, with SK hynix off 10.09%. [5]

The IMF's Global Financial Stability Report, out the same day, named an AI-driven correction one of three salient risks beside a sharp rise in sovereign yields and further cyber threats. [7] It counts 14 circular deals since 2023 in which hyperscalers put about $300 billion of equity into weaker AI firms, plus $650 billion of debt, for $1.4 trillion of revenue commitments. [6] Broadcom's Hock Tan said on Monday 12 October that many AI investors have 'no clue' what they are buying, likening the boom to a casino. [3]

Rates eased but stay high: the 10-year yield fell 2.7 basis points to 5.22% ahead of September CPI on Wednesday 14 October, seen at 3.6–3.7% on the year, and the Fed's Collins and Williams backed one more hike this year. [2] A WSJ survey of 71 economists found most expect the 10-year above 5%, with Allen Sinai seeing 6% next year. [8] Why 78: the score holds because the US close was flat rather than a break, while the IMF's circular-debt count, a 5% yield and another chip selloff keep pressure Critical. [1][2][6]
